<meta>continues from previous page. The text describes the wonders of music and its effects on nature, the mind, and the body.</meta><margin>The power of music</margin>
<unclear>St</unclear>agnum, proceeding from the mainland, move in a circle and lead a dance, then return to the shores. <note>Marcus</note> Varro testifies that he saw these things. And there are things more wonderful than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a lyre. At Megara, a certain rock, when struck, plays music like a stringed instrument; such is the great power of music. It soothes the soul itself, elevates the mind, incites warriors to battle, and relieves the labors and fatigue of every individual task. It recalls those who have fallen and those who are desperate, and comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by their singing drivers. In a similar way, those carrying heavy burdens sing, and they are empowered and lightened by it: for song produces pleasure and dexterity. It mitigates the angry, makes the sad and anxious joyful, reconciles those in discord, tempers the madness of the frantic, and scatters vain thoughts. Hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that certain diseases of the body and mind can be either cured or induced in this way. Thus we read of Terpander and Arion of <unclear>Methymna</unclear>

<summary>This passage details the marvelous effects of music on the natural world, human emotions, and physical health, citing authorities like Varro, Democritus, and Theophrastus.</summary>
<keywords>Music, Marcus Varro, Democritus, Theophrastus, Terpander, Arion, psychology, healing, therapeutic effects</keywords>
